skeleton:
Seven-Vegetable Couscous

Moroccan · Medium · Serves 6–8

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The Friday couscous is Morocco's weekly communion: the whole family at the table, the couscoussier's two stories working — the stew simmering below, the grain steaming above, and the steam of one perfuming the other through the pot's pierced lid. Seven is the traditional count of the vegetables (a count honored in its breach — the market decides), and the dish's craft is three clocks kept at once: the stew's long murmur, the grain's three steamings, and the vegetables' late entry. Served inverted on the great platter, the couscous crowned with the vegetables in their ring, it is this site's greatest single-plate record.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The stew (the bottom story)

The seven vegetables (the count, in the market's order)

The couscous (the top story)

- **Soak the chickpeas the night before — they join the stew whole and need their full tenderness.** The instant couscous bridges honestly (follow its steam-anyway: even "instant" improves with the pot's perfume), but the rolled grain's three steamings is the tradition's own craft. - **The bridge:** the couscoussier itself is the one tool — the two-story steamer. A stockpot with a colander sealed to its rim (a damp towel's ring makes the seal) bridges truly; the fallback of pot-then-grain is honest but loses the perfume's return.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The stew: deep-brothed, meat at the bone's yield, chickpeas tender.
  • The vegetables: staggered, each holding its form for the ring.
  • The grain: three steamings, three workings, distinct and perfumed.

Seven-Vegetable Couscous

Prep: 45 minutes · Cook: 1 hour 30 minutes · Total: About 2 hours 20 minutes · Serves 6–8

Ingredients

The stew (the bottom story)

  • 500 g lamb or beef on the bone (shank, neck, short rib), cut to 5 cm pieces
  • 2 onions (about 300 g), one sliced thin, one grated; 4 cloves garlic (about 15 g), sliced
  • 1 tsp saffron (about 1 g), steeped in 3 tbsp hot water (#120); 2 tsp ginger; 1 tsp turmeric; 1 tsp white pepper; ½ tsp cinnamon; 1 tbsp tomato paste (about 15 g)
  • 2 preserved lemon pulps (#92) or 1 whole lemon's juice; 100 g chickpeas, soaked 8 hours; 3 tbsp olive oil (about 40 g); 2 tsp salt; a fist of cilantro and parsley (about 30 g), tied
  • 2 litres water

The seven vegetables (the count, in the market's order)

  • 2 carrots (about 200 g), halved lengthwise; 2 turnips (about 300 g), quartered
  • ½ a small cabbage (about 300 g), in wedges; 2 zucchini (about 300 g), halved
  • 1 large potato (about 250 g) and 1 sweet potato or pumpkin quarter (about 250 g), in large pieces
  • 1 bunch coriander stems or 2 celery stalks (the seventh, argued, and honest either way)

The couscous (the top story)

  • 500 g medium couscous (the rolled grain — not the instant's promise); 2 tbsp olive oil (about 25 g); 1 tsp salt; butter (about 40 g) for the final working

Instructions

  1. **The stew's first hour.** Brown the meat lightly in the oil; add the onions, garlic, spices, tomato paste, and preserved lemon; 3 minutes to the pot's perfume. The water, the chickpeas, the herb bundle, and the salt — bring to the barest tremble (95 °C), cover, and simmer 1 hour, until the meat is nearly tender and the broth runs deep. Checkpoint — the broth at the hour: deep gold-brown, saffron-scented, one notch under final salt (the vegetables will calm it). The chickpeas should be tender to the bite's center.
  2. **The vegetables' staggered entry (25 minutes).** Add the carrots and turnips first; 10 minutes, then the cabbage and the seventh's celery or coriander stems; 10 more, and finally the zucchini, potato, and pumpkin — 5 to 8 minutes only, each vegetable to its own tenderness, all holding their shapes. Checkpoint — the law of the late vegetables: every piece must hold its form on the platter — a dissolved vegetable has missed its clock. Taste each kind at its pull: carrot tender-firm, zucchini just yielding, potato at the fork's edge. Lift all the vegetables to a warm bowl; the meat stays in the broth.
  3. **The couscous's three steamings (while the stew runs).** Work the dry couscous with the oil and a cup of the stew's broth, rubbing the grains apart between the palms; steam it over the stew 10 minutes. Turn it out, salt it, work it again with a cup of broth and let it drink 5 minutes; steam 10 more. A third time — the last working with butter, the grains rubbed to separate — and steam 10 final minutes, until the couscous is twice its dry volume, each grain distinct and tender. Checkpoint — the three-steam law: each steaming sets and swells the grain, and each working separates what the steam has joined — the couscous should end light, distinct, and never pasty, its perfume unmistakably the stew's own. This is the craft the instant grain never learned.
  4. **The assembly — the great platter.** The couscous mounded to the platter's center, a ladle of broth worked through it; a well made at the crown's center, the meat set in it; the vegetables arranged in their ring — each kind in its own arc — around; more broth poured at the table until the platter's edge drinks, the reserved broth's cup beside. Checkpoint — eating test, everyone from the platter's shared expanse: the couscous's perfumed lightness soaked with the broth's depth, a vegetable and a piece of meat in the same scoop — the cabbage's silk against the carrot's sweet-firm, the pumpkin's gold against the chickpea's earth — the preserved lemon's register running through the whole. It should taste like Friday: the week's work ending in the week's one certain plate.

Finish & Plate

The great platter to the table's center — the crown of meat, the ring of vegetables, the broth's ladle at the diner's own hand — and everyone eating from the shared expanse, which is the dish's oldest instruction.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Couscous pasty, denseUnder-worked or under-steamedThe three workings, the three steamings
Vegetables dissolvedAll in at onceThe staggered clock — roots first, gourds last
Broth weak, thinMeat under-stewed or water over-runThe hour before the vegetables; the 2 litres' measure

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The stew keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves (the Friday pot running into the week — the canon's own economy); the couscous is steamed to the day, though the leftover grain re-steams passably. The stew freezes 2 months as the canon's mother-broth. - Variations: the tfaya-crowned sweet version, the fish-brothed coastal one. This record is the canon's master; the #57 berkoukes and the #70's osban service are its family's other seats on this site.
